summary: The developer machine has the essential runtime, the DocumentDB MCP server, and a comprehensive set of DocumentDB skills installed, so a builder can start the Python LangChain sanctions-screening sample now. Key cold-answer inaccuracies were found (resource type, CLI group, billing model, connection URI form, vector index syntax, local dev image, underlying engine, and a few others) and have authoritative Microsoft Learn pages to correct them. Missing CLIs (azd, bicep, terraform) are non-blocking; mongosh is not on PATH and would help manual verification. Remaining information gaps are embedding model choice/dimensions and scoring thresholds for combining vector and regex signals — the sample must pick or document those before seed/index creation.
summary_points: Build can start: python, pip, az, Docker, node/npx, the documentdb MCP server and Microsoft Learn search are available and suitable for an end-to-end build and verification against the live cluster — verdict is ready_with_gaps.

Major cold-answer errors were detected: the correct ARM/Bicep resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), the CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster (not only az cosmosdb), and the service uses vCore compute tiers (M-series), not RU billing.

Vector search uses DocumentDB's cosmosSearch vector indexes (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann) created via createIndexes/cosmosSearch, not MongoDB's knnVector syntax; docs show example templates and $search usage.

Local development should use the DocumentDB local gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) on port 10260, not a vanilla mongo:7.0 image; SRV-style connection strings (mongodb+srv) are the normal cluster form.
Missing or optional tools: mongosh is not installed (useful for manual checks) and azd/bicep/terraform are not on PATH (helpful for infra but not required for this sample).

Information gaps that the builder must decide and document: embedding model/provider and embedding dimension, scoring/thresholds for combining vector similarity and regex signals, and seed dataset size and provenance.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource type name: databaseAccounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Current resource type for managed Mongo clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared historic name 'DocumentDB' and shared resource-provider namespace; older Cosmos DB account APIs use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and the Mongo API under Cosmos used that resource type.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep templates, they'll target the wrong resource type and either fail provisioning or create a Cosmos DB RU-based account instead of the vCore mongoClusters.
improvements: Add a note on the DocumentDB landing page that the cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and explicitly contrast it with Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB).
Update the agent kit 'documentdb-azure-deployment' skill readme to highlight the correct resource type and show example Bicep for mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create a MongoDB API account: az cosmosdb create -n my-docdb -g my-rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. This is in the core az CLI (az cosmosdb).
confusions.grounded_answer: The Azure CLI exposes dedicated commands for mongo clusters under 'az documentdb mongocluster' (and there is also an alias-style command group 'az cosmosdb mongocluster' in some docs). The 'az documentdb' command group (az documentdb mongocluster create) is the documented current group for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
az cosmosdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both 'az cosmosdb' and 'az documentdb' command groups may expose mongocluster subcommands in different docs or CLI versions; older Cosmos DB account commands used 'az cosmosdb'.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong az command group might call the Cosmos DB account APIs or fail if the command group isn't available in the installed CLI/extension; infra commands in the sample README would be wrong or fail.
improvements: Document the preferred CLI group (az documentdb mongocluster) and include both variants and a note about potential CLI extension aliases.
Add a short paragraph in the agent kit indicating which az CLI version and extensions are required to manage mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource type name in HCL: azurerm_cosmosdb_account).
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM and Terraform should target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). Use the mongoClusters templates and the AzAPI/Terraform modules for mongoClusters (not the generic databaseAccounts resource for this vCore mongoClusters deployment).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Azure used databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB resources, and earlier Mongo API docs used that; the new managed mongo vCore product uses a distinct resource type 'mongoClusters'.

confusion_sources.title: Bicep/Terraform examples for databaseAccounts (older Cosmos DB)

confusions.build_risk: Infra templates targeting databaseAccounts will not provision the correct vCore mongoClusters resource and will mis-configure indexes and capabilities the sample expects.
improvements: Add migration guidance on the deployment docs and agent-kit that shows how to convert databaseAccounts templates to mongoClusters templates and a recommended Terraform AzAPI snippet.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical connection string for the MongoDB-compatible Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos account: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. You can also get an SRV URI: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true. Username is often in the form <dbuser>@<account> and TLS/SSL must be enabled.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings use mongodb+srv scheme for cluster/global strings and have hostnames like <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com. The recommended options include tls=true (TLS), authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC (for Entra auth), retryWrites=false and maxIdleTimeMS set; SRV URIs are preferred for clients. The older :10255 URI form and the exact username format described map to older Cosmos DB Mongo API variants and are not the canonical form for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Enable private access in Azure DocumentDB (Get connection string to connect)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Similarity of hostnames and historic Cosmos DB Mongo endpoints (which used *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255) led the cold answer to conflate the managed mongoClusters SRV host and older Cosmos/Mongo API forms.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB (older) connection string docs showing port 10255

confusions.build_risk: Using an incorrect host/port or options can cause connection failures, TLS errors, or auth failures; SRV form plus proper TLS/auth options is required to connect reliably.
improvements: On the getting-started quickstarts, add a clear example that the cluster uses SRV hostnames like <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and list the minimal options for pymongo and mongosh.
In the sample README require builders to set DOCUMENTDB_URI with the SRV-style connection string and point to the 'how to connect' doc.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is usually billed in Request Units (RUs) for Cosmos DB accounts (provisioned RU/s or autoscale RU/s); there is also a serverless option for some accounts. (Note: some managed MongoDB offerings or dedicated SKUs may expose vCore-like tiers, but the default Cosmos / DocumentDB billing model is RU-based or serverless.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible service) is billed by compute tier (vCores in M-series like M10/M20/M30), storage and optional HA/replica compute; it does not use the Cosmos DB RU model. The RU model applies to Azure Cosmos DB RU-based accounts (the separate Cosmos DB for NoSQL and RU-mode MongoDB services).

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The old 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos DB' naming history and both being NoSQL document services confuse RU-based Cosmos DB and the new vCore-based DocumentDB products.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB request units documentation

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based provisioning they will pick the wrong cluster sizing model and supply wrong guidance in the README; indexing and throughput behaviors differ across models.
improvements: Add a clear note in the quickstart and sample README: 'This sample uses the vCore-based Azure DocumentDB (M-series) cluster; do not attempt to manage throughput via RUs.'
Update any onboarding docs that still use 'DocumentDB' ambiguously to explain vCore vs RU models.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane (MongoDB protocol) normally uses username/password credentials (SCRAM); for Cosmos DB the username is often <user>@<account> and the password is the primary key or a user password. Management operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) credentials via Azure RBAC. Direct MongoDB driver authentication via Microsoft Entra ID is not the usual path for data-plane reads/writes; the driver uses the connection string with user/password/primary key. (If Azure AD authentication for the MongoDB API exists it is a special preview feature and requires specific token-exchange steps rather than a standard SCRAM URI.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM authentication (username/password) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication for the data plane. Driver-based Microsoft Entra ID authentication is supported via MONGODB-OIDC (mongodb+srv ... ?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC) and managed identities can be registered; the docs show the required authMechanismProperties and SRV-URI patterns. Management plane uses Azure RBAC as usual.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control (MongoDB Compass example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical expectations that Mongo drivers only use SCRAM and that Azure AD is management-plane only; DocumentDB has explicit OIDC support and managed-identity patterns for data-plane connections.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID isn't supported they may omit code/examples showing how to connect with managed identities or MONGODB-OIDC; for a sample that targets enterprise patterns this omission is material.
improvements: Add an explicit example in the quickstart showing both (1) connection via DOCUMENTDB_URI with SCRAM credentials and (2) an example SRV string that demonstrates MONGODB-OIDC for managed identity or OIDC client-id login.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers for application data access (for Python use pymongo or motor). There is no separate data-plane 'DocumentDB' driver for Mongo workloads — use the MongoDB-compatible driver. For management (create account, keys, indexes via Azure) use azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / az CLI.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo/motor) for data-plane operations. For management/infrastructure tasks use the Azure management plane (az, ARM/Bicep/Terraform, or the mongoClusters ARM resource); the docs and quickstarts show pymongo examples.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None if standard drivers are used as recommended.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: On MongoDB 7-style vector support the index is a knnVector index; methods include HNSW (common) and other methods (IVF/DiskANN in some deployments). Example createIndex (Mongo shell / pymongo): db.sanctions.createIndex({embedding: "knnVector"}, {knnVector: {dimensions: 1536, method: "hnsw", M: 16, efConstruction: 200}}).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes created with the cosmosSearch kind via createIndexes: vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, and vector-diskann (DiskANN recommended for very large corpora). The index JSON uses a cosmosSearchOptions block and queries use $search with the cosmosSearch operator. The service does not use the MongoDB 'knnVector' createIndex syntax — use the cosmosSearch createIndexes payload.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search guidance and examples)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (IVF example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recalled MongoDB's native knnVector syntax (used in community or specific Mongo versions/patches) rather than the DocumentDB-specific 'cosmosSearch' vector index creation format.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses knnVector syntax the createIndex call will fail; the sample must use the DocumentDB createIndexes/cosmosSearch construction and match dimensions to the embedding model.
improvements: In the vector-search skill and quickstarts, show an explicit createIndexes JSON example for vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann with recommended parameters and dimension placeholders.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes ($text) or regex queries for lexical matching; vector search is performed via the vector index (knn). Hybrid search is implemented in the application by combining results from a vector similarity query (top-N from knn) and a text/regex/$text query, then merging/scoring results in application logic. There is no single built-in unified "vector + text" operator in Cosmos' MongoDB API (unlike Atlas Search) unless the service exposes a specialized search integration.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides search index capabilities via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage; it supports BM25 full-text search and vector search (cosmosSearch), and best-practice guidance explicitly describes hybrid patterns and combining BM25 with vector retrieval (including Reciprocal Rank Fusion guidance in docs/skills). While merging in-app is a valid pattern, DocumentDB's $search/cosmosSearch family provides richer text/vector tools and index types than plain $text.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (use LLM orchestration & full-text guidance)
Full text / createSearchIndexes guidance (documentdb-full-text-search skill)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer captured a generic hybrid-search pattern (vector + text) but missed that Azure DocumentDB provides $search/cosmosSearch and createSearchIndexes primitives (BM25 + vector) rather than relying solely on application-side merging of $text + vector results.
confusions.build_risk: Using only $text + post-merge will miss DocumentDB-specific $search features and performance optimizations; the sample should use $search/cosmosSearch and demonstrate recommended hybrid ranking patterns.
improvements: Add a small 'hybrid search' recipe in the vector-search docs showing $search usages that combine BM25 and cosmosSearch vectors and a short example of Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported server/wire versions depend on the account configuration; modern managed MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB/Cosmos accounts can present MongoDB 6.0/7.0 wire protocol compatibility if chosen at account creation. However, some MongoDB server features may be missing or limited (server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, some aggregation pipeline stages or storage-engine specific features). Expect subtle behavioral differences because the service translates Mongo protocol to the underlying engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol/server versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (explicitly documented). It supports ~99% of MongoDB operators but some admin commands or server-side-only features are not present; the official compatibility matrix lists supported operators and stages and which are excluded.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility summary)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was noncommittal; authoritative docs now state explicitly which wire versions are supported, including 8.0 in current docs.
confusions.build_risk: If builder assumes too-old compatibility they may avoid using features that are actually supported or write compatibility tests unnecessarily restrictive.
improvements: Update the sample checklist to specify the MongoDB wire protocol version the chosen cluster exposes (e.g., 7.0) and link to the compatibility matrix.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For local development run a standard MongoDB Docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) and use port 27017: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 ... Note: the Azure Cosmos DB emulator historically supports the Core (SQL) API and may not fully emulate the MongoDB API; when the emulator lacks the Mongo API use local MongoDB instead and test against the live cluster for service-specific features like vector indexes.
confusions.grounded_answer: For DocumentDB development use the DocumentDB local gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the gateway on port 10260 and supports DocumentDB features; the portal/quickstart docs provide the run and connection examples. A plain mongo:7.0 image will not emulate DocumentDB-specific features like vector indexes, createSearchIndexes, or Entra OIDC flows.

grounding_links.title: development-loop: start DocumentDB local gateway (docker run, port 10260)
DocumentDB on Azure Local quickstart (port-forward examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model defaulted to generic MongoDB local instructions instead of the DocumentDB-provided gateway image and port (10260) documented for local development.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB official docker images and standard 27017 port

confusions.build_risk: Using mongo:7.0 for local dev will hide DocumentDB-specific behaviors (vector search, cosmosSearch index creation, SRV semantics and port differences), leading to surprises when running against the live cluster.
improvements: In the 'documentdb-local-deployment' skill and quickstarts, emphasize the gateway image and port 10260 and add a short 'differences from vanilla mongo' section.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are a MongoDB feature and are supported only when the service exposes a replica-set style topology that implements the necessary oplog semantics. On managed DocumentDB/Cosmos Mongo API accounts change streams may be supported for certain compatibility versions but might need to be enabled or the account configured appropriately; if unsupported you'll need to poll or use service-specific change capture tools. (I would treat change streams as "possibly supported, check account settings".)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams. For multishard clusters a feature 'Change streams for multishard clusters' must be enabled (portal/Features) and there are documented prerequisites. The docs include how to enable and use change streams and examples for watch/Model.watch().

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Mongoose on Azure DocumentDB (Model.watch guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a — the cold answer was cautious but accurate in practice.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder doesn't enable the multishard change streams feature when needed for multishard clusters they won't receive cluster-wide change events.
improvements: Add a short 'enable change streams' checklist to the sample README if the sample uses them (how to enable in portal and prerequisites).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (the environment mentions a documentdb MCP server named 'documentdb'). The general Azure MCP server does not provide MongoDB data-plane tooling; use the documentdb-specific MCP server for data-plane inspect/index/query tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, explain, aggregate, etc.) for inspecting and verifying the live cluster. The general Azure MCP server is for control-plane Azure resource ops but not the document-level data-plane commands shown in the documentdb server.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (installed data-plane tools)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None; the documentdb MCP server is installed and must be used for data-plane verification.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had a service named Azure DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. "DocumentDB" as a name was the original document store offering and Cosmos DB is the successor umbrella service offering multiple APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra-compatible, Gremlin, Table). The open-source 'DocumentDB' project is unrelated; Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is Microsoft's proprietary managed service that exposes a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol for the Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but confusing: the name 'DocumentDB' used historically for the original Microsoft service that became Azure Cosmos DB (in 2017) — separate from the newer 'Azure DocumentDB' vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible service. The current Azure DocumentDB (vCore) product is distinct from Cosmos DB RU model and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed as an OSS project). Also, 'Amazon DocumentDB' is a separate AWS service and should not be conflated. The docs explicitly call out these distinctions.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (naming and relationship to Cosmos DB)
DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical renames and the reuse of the 'DocumentDB' string across products and the existence of a separate open-source DocumentDB project cause name collisions.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB historical docs (legacy DocumentDB)

confusions.build_risk: Name confusion in docs or sample README could cause a builder to pick the RU-based Cosmos DB account or to attempt CLI commands for the wrong service.
improvements: In the agent kit and sample README, add a short paragraph 'Which DocumentDB is this sample for?' that explicitly states: 'This sample targets Azure DocumentDB (vCore mongoClusters), not Azure Cosmos DB RU-mode or Amazon DocumentDB.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is the Cosmos DB proprietary distributed storage/engine when this is the Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB managed service; it implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top. That can change behavior: indexing, consistency, transactions, performance characteristics and some commands differ from a native MongoDB server, so expect subtle compatibility differences even when using standard MongoDB drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the current Azure DocumentDB (vCore) product the underlying engine is the open-source 'DocumentDB' engine (built on PostgreSQL via pg_documentdb extensions) which Microsoft has open sourced. Application code remains MongoDB-driver-compatible, but the underlying engine is not the MongoDB server; some admin/ops features or edge-case behaviors can differ. The docs explicitly call out that DocumentDB is built on an open-source engine.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (engine and portability)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB-based DocumentDB used a proprietary engine; the new vCore-managed service uses the open-source DocumentDB engine, causing the memory to substitute the proprietary engine for the new product.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB internal engine guidance (older docs)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the Cosmos engine behavior they may mis-expect certain operational features; conversely knowing it's an open-source engine can help when preparing local operator or offline test strategies.
improvements: Add a short 'engine' section on the sample README stating that DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine and link to the GitHub repo and OSS docs.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a knnVector index on the embedding field. Example (Mongo shell): db.sanctions.createIndex({embedding: "knnVector"}, {knnVector: {dimensions: 1536, method: "hnsw", M: 16, efConstruction: 200}}).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use DocumentDB's createIndexes payload for cosmosSearch vector indexes, e.g. kind 'vector-hnsw', 'vector-ivf' or 'vector-diskann' with a cosmosSearchOptions block containing dimensions and algorithm-specific parameters (m, efConstruction, numLists, etc.). The sample must set dimensions to the chosen embedding model's output size. Example templates and $search usage are provided in the vector-search docs.

confusions.question: How should the Python app connect to the DocumentDB cluster at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string from environment DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to pymongo. Example: from pymongo import MongoClient; import os; uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']; client = MongoClient(uri, tls=True) — ensure TLS/ssl is enabled and the username/password from the URI are valid for the account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Read DOCUMENTDB_URI from environment and pass to pymongo. Preferred cluster forms are SRV (mongodb+srv://<user>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000). Use singleton MongoClient, set TLS options as required, and respect authMechanism= MONGODB-OIDC if using Microsoft Entra ID. The docs show quickstart Python/Node examples and portal connection-string guidance.

confusions.question: What non-vector indexes does this sample need for regex and text matching?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a text index on name and alias fields plus a b-tree index on normalized fields used for regex. Example: db.sanctions.createIndex({name: "text", aliases: "text"}); db.sanctions.createIndex({name_normalized: 1});
confusions.grounded_answer: Create a text index (one text index per collection) on the fields used for full-text matching and create standard single-field or compound b-tree indexes on normalized fields used in regex or prefix lookups. DocumentDB docs recommend using custom analyzers and textSearch features for richer behavior and a separate normalized field for fast prefix searches.

confusions.question: Which port will the live cluster use and what port should local fallback use in tests?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure-managed MongoDB-compatible accounts typically listen on TLS port 10255 (or via SRV with default TLS ports). For local fallback during development use the standard MongoDB port 27017 (e.g. mongo:7.0 Docker image).
confusions.grounded_answer: For DocumentDB clusters the normal managed gateway listens via SRV hostnames (mongodb+srv) to the cluster's global hostname; the local DocumentDB gateway image listens on port 10260 for local testing. The older Cosmos DB Mongo API port 10255 is a different historical endpoint and should not be assumed for the vCore mongoClusters or local gateway. For multi-node 'query from any node' scenarios the cluster may expose additional ports starting at 10260 for each physical shard.

confusions.question: How will the sample authenticate when run in the developer environment?
confusions.cold_answer: For the sample use the connection string credentials (username/password) in DOCUMENTDB_URI; do not attempt Azure AD authentication from the MongoDB driver. Create an account-level or database user in the cluster and embed those credentials in the URI provided at runtime (kept in environment only).
confusions.grounded_answer: For a developer sample the simplest path is to use DOCUMENTDB_URI with a SCRAM username/password credential. However DocumentDB also supports Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for the data plane and managed identities; the sample can document both options. The docs show SRV URIs that use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for Entra flows.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the ARM/Bicep resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) when authoring deployment templates for the vCore-managed DocumentDB service.

Use the 'az documentdb mongocluster' CLI commands (az documentdb mongocluster create / show / firewall-rule list) for cluster management in examples; include the az cosmosdb mongocluster alias note if you add CLI instructions.

Create vector indexes using DocumentDB's createIndexes/cosmosSearch JSON (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, or vector-diskann) and set 'dimensions' to match your chosen embedding model; do not use MongoDB 'knnVector' syntax.
